Meritorious

/mair-ih-TOR-ee-uss/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Meritorious means deserving of praise or reward because of genuine merit or achievement.

The judges reserved the top prize for truly meritorious work, not merely polished work.

Worked Example

For two summers, Owen mapped every storm drain in the flood-prone east side, then built a free app that warned residents which streets would flood first. The city engineer admitted the teenager's data was better than the county's. When the mayor's office looked for meritorious projects to fund, Owen's app was first on the list — it had earned its place through real, measurable achievement.

Owen's app earns the label meritorious because the recognition rests on genuine, demonstrated achievement — two summers of work that measurably protects his neighbors.

How Meritorious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

praiseworthy

praiseworthy: deserving praise

admirable

admirable: worthy of respect and approval

Antonyms

shameful

shameful: deserving blame or disgrace

undeserving

undeserving: not having earned the reward

How Strong Is It? — decent → meritorious → heroic

decent vs. meritorious

decent vs. meritorious: Decent work is acceptable; meritorious work rises above that — good enough to genuinely deserve praise or a reward.

heroic vs. meritorious

heroic vs. meritorious: Heroic goes beyond meritorious, suggesting achievement at real personal risk or sacrifice.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — merit

Root — merit: earned, deserved (Latin merere, 'to earn')

Suffix — -orious

Suffix — -orious: characterized by; full of

Put it together

Put it together: Meritorious grows straight out of the Latin verb merere, 'to earn or deserve' — the root you already know from merit itself and from meritocracy, a system where rewards are earned. Add the adjective suffix -orious and the word means 'full of earned worth': praise that the achievement itself has paid for.

Use the root in a new word: meritocracy

Use the root in a new word: meritocracy: In a meritocracy, positions are earned by ability and achievement — the same Latin root merere, 'to earn,' that makes meritorious work worth rewarding.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal; common in awards, citations, and official praise

Meritorious focuses on whether the achievement itself has earned reward — it describes the deed, whereas a commendation (also in this unit) is the official document or statement of praise that a meritorious deed might receive.
